subject: Wages up 2%, prices up 3%, 42,000 jobs gone
bodyMarkdown:
If you are asking for a raise this fall, or wondering when your mortgage renewal gets cheaper, Friday's jobs report from Statistics Canada is the one to read. Canadian pay is now growing at 2.0 per cent a year while prices are growing at 3.0 per cent.

## What the August report said

Statistics Canada reported on Friday, September 4, that employment fell by 42,000 in August and the unemployment rate held at 6.4 per cent. Economists had expected a gain of about 15,000, so the miss was close to 57,000 positions. The employment rate, the share of working age Canadians who actually hold a job, slipped a tenth of a point to 60.8 per cent. Youth aged 15 to 24 lost 19,000 jobs, and their unemployment rate sat at 12.9 per cent, roughly double the national figure. Manufacturing was the odd bright spot with a gain of 22,000, while business, building and other support services shed 20,000 and public administration lost 9,000. When the jobless rate holds steady and jobs disappear anyway, it usually means people stopped looking for work.

## Pay is losing to prices

Average hourly wages rose 2.0 per cent from a year earlier in August, down from 2.8 per cent in July and 3.3 per cent in June. Statistics Canada put July inflation at 3.0 per cent, driven mostly by gasoline, which was up 25.7 per cent from a year earlier. So the average Canadian worker took a real pay cut of about a point last month, and workers at the bottom took a bigger one. FX.co reported that pay for the lowest earning quarter of workers grew just 1.1 per cent. Two straight months of deceleration like that is not a rounding error. Employers cut hiring first, then hours, then raises, and we are at the third stage now. My read is that Canadian workers quietly lost their bargaining power sometime this summer, and the data is only catching up.

## None of this includes the tariffs yet

Here is the timing gap. The survey's **reference week**, the seven days respondents are asked to describe, ran from August 9 to 15. The United States put a 50 per cent tariff on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods on August 22, after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with Washington. Canada's matching counter tariffs on the same value of American goods take effect Tuesday. So the August report describes a labour market that had not yet been touched by any of it. CBC News quoted CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham on Friday saying the data would not capture the tariff shock because the survey is taken mid month. Whatever a 50 per cent rate does to sawmills and distillers will land in next month's report.

## The takeaway

The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2 for the seventh straight decision and said the risks to inflation are tilted to the upside, so one weak jobs print will not buy anyone a cut on October 28. If you are negotiating pay this fall, treat 2.0 per cent as the going rate and argue from what you specifically did, because the labour market will not argue for you. If you are a student in Ontario heading back to class, plan around a youth unemployment rate of 12.9 per cent instead of last year's. The number I am waiting on is next month's jobs report, the first one that will actually contain the tariffs.
